rationale: Detects unusual AI behavior and performance shifts in production (MEASURE 2.4), surfaces emergent risks for tracking (MEASURE 3.1), and is a core mechanism of the post-deployment monitoring plan (MANAGE 4.1).

Real-time monitoring of model performance, drift, and bias is the production monitoring MEASURE 2.4 requires, tracks existing and emergent risks over time (MEASURE 3.1), and implements the post-deployment monitoring plan (MANAGE 4.1).

Identifies AI-native indicators of compromise such as adversarial prompts, which monitors system behavior in production (MEASURE 2.4) and supplies evidence for evaluating AI security and resilience (MEASURE 2.7).

Provides the practices for identifying AI incidents (GOVERN 4.3), responding to and recovering from newly identified risks (MANAGE 2.3), and tracking, communicating, and recovering from incidents and errors (MANAGE 4.3).
Independent testing of digital and AI environments involves assessors outside the development team (MEASURE 1.3) and evaluates AI system security and resilience (MEASURE 2.7).
Integrates AI-specific threat intelligence through information-sharing practices (GOVERN 4.3) to identify and track emergent adversarial risks (MEASURE 3.1).
Visible leadership commitment is executive responsibility for AI risk decisions (GOVERN 2.3), and its resource allocation accounts for the resources required to manage AI risks (MANAGE 2.1).
Chartered oversight bodies document roles, responsibilities, and lines of communication for AI risk (GOVERN 2.1) and bring a diverse, multidisciplinary group into AI risk decisions (GOVERN 3.1).
Board-level oversight provides the periodic review of the AI risk management process with defined roles (GOVERN 1.5) and executive responsibility for AI risk decisions (GOVERN 2.3).

Assigns a traceable human owner with authority to act on AI risk findings, which documents AI risk roles and responsibilities (GOVERN 2.1) and differentiates roles for human-AI configurations and oversight (GOVERN 3.2).
Quantitative fairness metrics evaluate and document fairness and bias (MEASURE 2.11), and mitigating identified disparities is a planned response to high-priority AI risks (MANAGE 1.3).
Inclusive practices put diverse teams into AI risk decisions (GOVERN 3.1), reflect demographic diversity in context-setting (MAP 1.2), and sustain engagement with affected stakeholders (MAP 5.2).

Respecting cultural norms and jurisdictional sensitivities documents context-specific norms and expectations (MAP 1.1) and connects measurement to the deployment context through consultation (MEASURE 4.1).

Documenting and justifying trade-offs among accuracy, privacy, and fairness examines the benefits (MAP 3.1) and costs, including non-monetary costs (MAP 3.2), of system functionality and trustworthiness.

Explainability statements and AI-use disclosures document knowledge limits and human use of outputs (MAP 2.2), address transparency and accountability risks (MEASURE 2.8), and explain model output in context (MEASURE 2.9).
Defines permissible and prohibited AI use for personnel, integrating trustworthy-AI expectations into policy (GOVERN 1.2) and fostering a safety-first mindset in AI use (GOVERN 4.1).

Establishes a culture of responsible data and AI use, integrating fairness, privacy, and accountability into organizational practice (GOVERN 1.2) and a critical-thinking, safety-first mindset (GOVERN 4.1).
Operationalizes human-centric principles such as fairness and explainability in policy and practice (GOVERN 1.2) and promotes a safety-first culture across the AI lifecycle (GOVERN 4.1).
A hierarchical policy architecture integrates trustworthy-AI characteristics into policy (GOVERN 1.2) and establishes the risk management process through transparent policies (GOVERN 1.4).
Enforceable security policy integrates the secure and resilient characteristic into organizational policy (GOVERN 1.2) and sets risk management expectations by policy (GOVERN 1.4).

Preparedness and recovery policies govern responding to and recovering from unknown risks (MANAGE 2.3), disengaging systems that behave inconsistently with intended use (MANAGE 2.4), and incident handling (MANAGE 4.3).

Principle-based AI policy integrates trustworthy characteristics (GOVERN 1.2), establishes the AI risk management process (GOVERN 1.4), and fosters a safety-first design and deployment culture (GOVERN 4.1).
Privacy policy integrates the privacy-enhanced characteristic into organizational policy (GOVERN 1.2) and defines how AI privacy risk is examined and documented (MEASURE 2.10).
Enforceable ethical standards integrate trustworthy-AI values into policy (GOVERN 1.2) and support a critical-thinking, safety-first culture (GOVERN 4.1).
Personnel practices define AI-related roles and responsibilities (GOVERN 2.1) and require AI risk management training for personnel and partners (GOVERN 2.2).
Supplier standards for AI software and datasets are the third-party AI risk policies GOVERN 6.1 requires and set the approach for mapping third-party component and legal risks (MAP 4.1).
Data-governance policy integrates data quality and lawful provenance into policy (GOVERN 1.2) and sets the data collection and selection considerations documented under MAP 2.3.
Turns policy commitments into measurable, auditable standards that embed trustworthy characteristics in procedures (GOVERN 1.2) and operationalize the risk management process (GOVERN 1.4).
Hardening standards for AI infrastructure define the internal risk controls for AI system components (MAP 4.2) against which security and resilience are evaluated (MEASURE 2.7).

Standardized AI failure-recovery processes include contingency handling for third-party failures (GOVERN 6.2), recovery from newly identified risks (MANAGE 2.3), and incident tracking and recovery (MANAGE 4.3).

Standards for data, model testing, and deployment monitoring select measurement approaches and metrics (MEASURE 1.1), document TEVV test sets and tools (MEASURE 2.1), and define production monitoring (MEASURE 2.4).
Compliance with data protection law requires legal and regulatory requirements to be understood and documented (GOVERN 1.1) and AI privacy risk to be examined (MEASURE 2.10).

IP management addresses the risk of infringing third-party intellectual property, which GOVERN 6.1 and MAP 4.1 name explicitly, and protects proprietary models, algorithms, and training data under documented legal-risk mapping (MAP 4.1).

Conformance to AI transparency and safety law requires AI legal and regulatory requirements to be understood, managed, and documented (GOVERN 1.1) and context-specific laws to be identified per system (MAP 1.1).
Aligning cybersecurity controls with legal and contractual obligations documents applicable requirements (GOVERN 1.1) and informs the security evaluation of AI systems (MEASURE 2.7).
Ethics and anti-discrimination compliance requires the applicable legal requirements to be documented (GOVERN 1.1) and fairness and bias to be evaluated with results documented (MEASURE 2.11).
Embedding ethical tenets in system design integrates trustworthy characteristics into policy and practice (GOVERN 1.2) and fosters a safety-first organizational culture (GOVERN 4.1).
The privacy program elicits privacy requirements for AI systems (MAP 1.6) and examines and documents AI privacy risk (MEASURE 2.10).
A unified risk framework sets the level of risk management by risk tolerance (GOVERN 1.3), establishes the process through transparent policy (GOVERN 1.4), and plans its periodic review (GOVERN 1.5).
Approved risk thresholds determine and document organizational risk tolerance (MAP 1.5) and set the level of risk management activity needed (GOVERN 1.3).

AI risk management across the lifecycle identifies impact likelihood and magnitude (MAP 5.1), selects risk metrics (MEASURE 1.1), prioritizes and plans risk responses (MANAGE 1.2, 1.3), and documents residual risk (MANAGE 1.4).
Cybersecurity risk analysis feeds the evaluation of AI system security and resilience (MEASURE 2.7) and the planned response to high-priority risks (MANAGE 1.3).
Third-party risk management is governed by third-party AI risk policies (GOVERN 6.1) and regularly monitors third-party AI risks and applies controls (MANAGE 3.1).
Precise technical boundaries specify the targeted application scope of each system (MAP 3.3) and identify the internal risk controls that apply to each component (MAP 4.2).
Aligning security and AI governance to the organization’s purpose documents the organization’s mission and goals for AI technology (MAP 1.3).
Risk-informed goals based on internal and external context document the deployment context (MAP 1.1) and the organization’s goals for AI (MAP 1.3).
Identifying and categorizing all in-scope AI systems relies on the AI inventory mechanism (GOVERN 1.6) and specifies each system’s application scope and categorization (MAP 3.3).
Proportionate protection based on criticality sets the level of risk management by risk tolerance (GOVERN 1.3) and identifies the internal controls for AI components (MAP 4.2).
Determining applicable legal and customer requirements documents AI legal and regulatory requirements (GOVERN 1.1) and context-specific laws per system (MAP 1.1).
A living inventory of AI components and metadata is the AI system inventory mechanism GOVERN 1.6 requires.

Evaluating AI impacts documents risks and potential impacts (GOVERN 4.2), examines potential costs and harms (MAP 3.2), identifies impact likelihood and magnitude (MAP 5.1), and gathers stakeholder feedback on impacts (MAP 5.2).
Systematic identification of AI, privacy, and safety risks documents risks and impacts (GOVERN 4.2), identifies their likelihood and magnitude (MAP 5.1), and tracks emergent risks (MEASURE 3.1).
Insider threat mitigation identifies internal controls protecting AI data and models (MAP 4.2) and contributes to evaluating AI security and resilience (MEASURE 2.7).
Managing software, model, and dataset supplier risk maps third-party component risks (MAP 4.1), monitors third-party resources (MANAGE 3.1), and monitors pre-trained models in use (MANAGE 3.2).
Measurable thresholds for drift, fairness, and safety document risk tolerance (MAP 1.5), define the metrics used (MEASURE 1.1), and trigger disengagement when outcomes exceed them (MANAGE 2.4).
Tracking threats to AI assets informs the security and resilience evaluation (MEASURE 2.7) and the tracking of emergent risks (MEASURE 3.1).

Embedding TEVV and governance from design to decommissioning documents TEVV considerations (MAP 2.3), gates go/no-go decisions (MANAGE 1.1), sustains deployed system value (MANAGE 2.2), and governs safe decommissioning (GOVERN 1.7).
Structured reporting to AI governance committees supports periodic review of the risk process (GOVERN 1.5) through documented lines of communication (GOVERN 2.1).
External AI audit provides independent assessment (MEASURE 1.3) and evaluates the effectiveness of TEVV metrics and processes (MEASURE 2.13).

Safe channels for reporting AI concerns collect and integrate feedback from outside the development team (GOVERN 5.1), feed adjudicated feedback into design (GOVERN 5.2), and give users a way to report problems and appeal outcomes (MEASURE 3.3).
Internal AI audit is a periodic review of the AI risk management process (GOVERN 1.5) by assessors independent of front-line developers (MEASURE 1.3).
Security and reliability testing documents test sets and tools (MEASURE 2.1), measures performance under deployment-like conditions (MEASURE 2.3), and evaluates security and resilience (MEASURE 2.7).

Evaluating performance and harms across operating contexts measures performance (MEASURE 2.3), validity and reliability (MEASURE 2.5), and safety (MEASURE 2.6), informed by domain-expert input (MEASURE 4.2).
Verifying that systems meet design and policy requirements measures performance and assurance criteria (MEASURE 2.3) and checks the effectiveness of the TEVV process itself (MEASURE 2.13).

Validation demonstrates the system is valid and reliable (MEASURE 2.5) with expert input on in-context performance (MEASURE 4.2), and supports the decision on whether the system achieves its purpose and should proceed (MANAGE 1.1).
